newsitem.title: GERMANY: German towns brace for worst as floodwaters arrive.
newsitem.headline: German towns brace for worst as floodwaters arrive.

text.p: Floods that have swept through central Europe this week claiming dozens of lives poured down the river dividing Germany and Poland on Thursday, putting villages under water for the first time in decades.

Residents of Ratzdorf, a village where the Oder and Neisse Rivers flow together about 80 km (50 miles) east of Berlin, said they had not seen such floods since 1947, the last time the river that is Germany's eastern border washed over its banks.

Dozens of people in the picturesque farming village were furiously filling sandbanks on Thursday even as the muddy brown water streamed into low-lying farmland and flooded into basements of houses nearby.

"Yesterday you could stand at the fence 100 metres from here," said Eberhard Wolf, a local resident surveying the fast-moving water that flooded his barn and was expected to crest another metre higher on Friday.
But the damage in Germany was slight compared to across the river in Poland, where police put the country's death toll so far at 46 from the floods that began with downpours early last week.
Poland has called a day of mourning for Friday. Waters were only just receding in the south, leaving a stench and a risk of disease in shattered streets veiled in sewage, rubbish and dead animals.
But German authorities were bracing for a wave of high water moving north along what the Germans call the Oder river and the Poles call the Odra.

Guenter Feister, a German aide worker, said over 30 volunteers were called out at 5 a.m. local time (0300 GMT) Thursday to build a wall of sandbanks near the river at Ratzdorf to prepare for the floodwaters.
He said the river was moving at a rate of five km per hour and would peak at nearly 7.5 metres above flood level by midday on Friday.

"Ratzdorf has never seen anything like this," said Ingetraud Wellkisch, 65, as she and her husband watched workers scurry to fill sandbags outside their farmhouse. She recalled the last major flood in 1947 and how townspeople paddled down the Ratzdorf's main street.
The Oder, usually about 200 metres from their front door, was closing in fast and just a few metres away. Tree trunks and dead animals had swept past the front window in recent days, they said.
"We expect this entire street to be covered with water tomorrow," Feister said.
In Frankfurt on the Oder, about 40 km (25 miles) to the north, the river had already flooded the Polish side and was threatening to spill its banks into the city of 80,000.
Hundreds of gawkers from as far away as Berlin drove to Frankfurt to watch the surging river.
"I just came to have a look -- everyone is curious, aren't they?" said Wolfgang Siepert, who drove out from Berlin.

One tavern in Frankfurt was offering beer at flood prices. Each time the water rises, the price of a half litre of beer is raised to match the river level, said the owner of the Oderspeicher tavern. It could reach 7 marks ($3.89) by Friday, but should quickly fall back to normal next week.
